title: I read the license terms of 30+ AI gamedev tools. Most free tiers can't go in a paid game, and some paid tiers can't either. Full table + sources
author: jonnygravity
selftext:
Not here to sell anyone on AI tools. If you don't use them, this post isn't for you, and that's fine.

But if you or a contractor puts AI output into something you sell, the plan it was generated on decides what you're allowed to do with it. The landing page usually doesn't tell you, and some of the fine print is pretty sneaky.

I went through the pricing pages, terms and help docs for 36 AI tools people use in gamedev. For every claim I saved the vendor's exact sentence plus the URL and date. 212 claims matched the live page when I re-checked them this week. 39 I couldn't pin down, and those are marked unverified below instead of guessed.

This is the asset side (art, 3D, audio, voice, NPC dialogue). Code tools get one line at the bottom.

**What actually surprised me**

* **Most free tiers can't ship in a paid game.** Tripo, Sloyd, Scenario, Luma, Cascadeur, Recraft, Suno, AIVA, Soundful, ElevenLabs, WellSaid and Rosebud all say non-commercial or personal use on free.
* **Upgrading later doesn't fix old output.** Luma: Free/Lite content is personal use only and the watermark "cannot be removed, even if you later upgrade your subscription." Luma and Recraft both tie commercial rights to stuff made *while subscribed*.
* **Paying isn't the same as being allowed to ship.**
   * AIVA Standard (€11/mo) is "limited monetization" on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok and Instagram, and AIVA keeps the copyright. You own it on Pro (€33/mo).
   * Mubert's pricing FAQ says Creator "is intended for non-commercial content." Pro ($39/mo) is labeled "Commercial Usage," but the same FAQ says to choose Ultra ($89/mo) for "music in apps or games." On every plan, their license page says "Mubert owns all the rights to the tracks generated."
   * Cascadeur Indie needs revenue or funding under $100k for the prior 12 months, checked at download and at every renewal.
   * Midjourney: if your business grosses over $1M a year you need Pro or Mega to use images commercially.
* **Free often means public.** Tripo free is the one that got me. Free models are public, and Tripo "retains all rights" in free users' outputs, including the right to license them and make money off them. Recraft free images go in a public gallery and Recraft owns them. Leonardo keeps a perpetual license to public images, and other users can use them too. God Mode AI's $29/mo plan is "up to 200 public generations."
* **"Commercial use" and "you own it" are different rows.** Meshy free is CC BY 4.0, so you can sell with credit, but Meshy owns the model. SOUNDRAW keeps the phonogram producer's neighboring rights and licenses the music to you. Sloyd gives you a license to use the models, not ownership. Charisma's TTS audio is sub-licensed, not yours.
* **Nobody promises it's original.** Meshy and Scenario both say they don't guarantee output is unique. Suno: "Suno makes no representation or warranty to you that any copyright will vest in any Output."

**The table** (checked Oct 15 to 21, 2026. Prices are what the page showed. Check before you rely on any of it.)

|Tool|Free tier commercial?|Cheapest plan that says commercial|Who owns output|The catch|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|**3D / animation**|||||
|Meshy (text/image to 3D models)|Yes, CC BY 4.0, credit Meshy|Free|Free: Meshy. Paid: you|No uniqueness guarantee|
|Tripo (text/image to 3D models)|No ("Non-Commercial Use")|Pro, $20/mo billed yearly|Free: Tripo. Paid: you|Free models are public. Paid users still let Tripo use/display outputs to run the service|
|Sloyd (text/image/template to 3D models)|No (personal-use license)|Plus, $15/mo|Licensed to you, not owned|Reselling models on an asset store is Pro only ($50/mo)|
|Scenario (game asset generator: 2D, 3D, audio)|No ("personal and evaluation use only")|Starter, $15/mo|Assigned to you|No guarantee it's unique, original or non-infringing|
|Hyper3D Rodin (image to 3D models)|Not stated|Business, $120/mo|Terms say they won't limit your use|Homepage FAQ doesn't say every generation is cleared|
|3D AI Studio (image/text to 3D, rigging)|Page doesn't split by plan|Not split (smallest paid: $34 one-time pack)|You|Free plan keeps models 6 months, paid 12. Download what you ship|
|Kaedim (3D asset production service)|Not tracked|Price not on the page I track|You|Deletion on request is a retention promise, not indemnity|
|Cascadeur (AI-assisted 3D character animation)|No (and .casc export only)|Pro, $49/mo ($33 yearly)|Unverified|Indie ($19, $8 yearly) has the under-$100k cap|
|**2D / images / video**|||||
|Luma AI (image and video generator)|No (personal use, watermark)|Plus, $30/mo|Assigned to you|Only output made during an active paid sub is commercial|
|Midjourney (image and video generator)|No free plan|Basic, $10/mo|You, even after you cancel|Over $1M/yr gross: Pro or Mega|
|Leonardo (image and video generator)|Yes, per their help article|Free|Private paid gens: you|Public images: Leonardo and other users get rights|
|Recraft (image and vector generator)|No, Recraft owns them|Basic (no $ in the page text)|Paid: you, survives cancel|Free images are public|
|Stability AI (Stable Diffusion, Stable Audio models)|Yes, under $1M annual revenue|Free Community License|You|Over $1M: Enterprise, custom price|
|PixelLab (pixel art sprites, tilesets, animations)|Yes (FAQ isn't plan-specific)|Price not tracked|You|Can't train models on outputs. Open RAIL-M applies|
|Layer (image, video, 3D, audio suite)|"Commercial license for all users"|$10/mo|You, if Layer has the rights|Unused units expire (10% rolls over)|
|God Mode AI (character image to sprite animations)|Not tracked|$29/mo|Unverified|Plan is "public generations." All purchases final|
|**Music**|||||
|Suno (song generator)|No rights, no downloads|Pro, $8/mo billed yearly|No promise any copyright vests|Only commercial if downloaded within your plan's allocation (Pro: 20/mo)|
|AIVA (music composition generator)|No, AIVA owns it, credit required|Pro, €33/mo + VAT (yearly)|Pro: you. Free/Standard: AIVA|Standard is socials-only monetization|
|Mubert (music generator)|Unverified|Ultra for games, $89/mo ($62.50 yearly)|Mubert|FAQ sends apps/games to Ultra, not Pro|
|SOUNDRAW (royalty-free music generator)|Not tracked|Creator, $16.99/mo ($11.04 yearly)|SOUNDRAW keeps neighboring rights|Creator is for individuals and companies under 10 employees|
|Soundful (royalty-free tracks and loops)|No (Personal License)|Premium (no $ in the page text)|You keep ownership, per their license page|Commercial needs an *active* premium plan|
|**Voice**|||||
|ElevenLabs (voice, SFX and music)|No|Starter, $6/mo|You (as between you and them)|Separate terms if you're in the EEA, Switzerland or UK|
|WellSaid (voiceover studio)|No ("no commercial rights")|Starter, $10/mo yearly or $19 monthly|Unverified|Starter is 20 downloaded minutes/mo|
|Cartesia (text-to-speech and voice agents)|Not in the Free list|Pro, $5/mo|Unverified||
|**NPC dialogue / game builders**|||||
|Inworld (realtime voice/LLM for characters)|"Commercial license" on the $0 pay-as-you-go column|Free / pay as you go|Outputs assigned to you|Service license is "solely for your internal business purposes"|
|Charisma.ai (interactive characters and stories)|Not tracked|Pro, $5 per 50k credits|Story owner owns output|Synthesized voice audio is sub-licensed|
|Rosebud (prompt-to-game builder)|No, incl. internal business use|Terms: any paid plan. FAQ: "10x Dev and higher"|Not stated. You grant them a perpetual, sublicensable license|Two of their own pages disagree on the tier. Cool|

Mubert note: Pro ($39/mo) is labeled "Commercial Usage," but the pricing FAQ says "Choose Ultra for client and agency work, music in apps or games." Their page was flipping between two versions earlier this week (the older one sent games to a $199 Business plan), so check it the day you buy.

**Code tools, one line:** GitHub Copilot, JetBrains AI and Unity AI don't claim ownership of your code. GitHub says output can match code under open-source licenses and that's on you. Copilot individual plans may train on your prompts and snippets unless you opt out.

**Steam is a separate check**

None of the above is Valve's rule. The Content Survey asks about "Pre-Generated" content: "Any kind of content that ships with your game and is consumed by players that is created with the help of AI tools during development." It also says efficiency gains from AI tools built into dev environments are "not the focus of this section." So Copilot in your IDE and a Suno track in your soundtrack land in different places. If content is generated live while the game runs (Inworld, Charisma style NPCs), the survey also asks what guardrails stop illegal output.

**What I couldn't verify**

Udio, Adobe Firefly and Convai: every commercial and ownership row is unverified. Either my checker couldn't fetch the page or I couldn't find a sentence that actually says it. Same for Ludo.ai's commercial terms, plus output ownership for Cascadeur, Cartesia, God Mode AI and WellSaid. If you know where a vendor actually states it, send the link.

**How I checked, and the limits**

* Every row is backed by a sentence copied from the vendor's own page (Valve's for the Steam part). A script re-downloads the page and checks the sentence is still there word for word. No LLM in that loop.
* A separate daily job diffs each pricing page and logs any change with the date. That's how Mubert's pricing page swapping versions showed up.
* I'm not a lawyer. This is what the vendor's own pages say, not whether a court would agree with them. Terms change. Check the plan you were on *when you generated the asset*.
* Practical thing that costs nothing: when you generate something you might ship, save the plan name and date with a screenshot of the terms, right next to the file.

**Disclosure:** I built a free site that tracks all this, RespawnStack. No signup, no affiliate links. The full table with the source link and copy date on every row is here: [https://respawnstack.com/guides/ai-game-dev-tools-commercial-use-table](https://respawnstack.com/guides/ai-game-dev-tools-commercial-use-table)

If a row's wrong, tell me which one and link the page. I'll fix it and log the date.

comments.body:
This is something people really need to pay attention to.

I'd also be interested in the actual technical controls.  The big dogs are watermarking their outputs, but id bet a lot of these smaller services are merely claiming they are and don't have any discernible watermarks, and no way are they keeping generative output indefinitely to try to claim they have rights to your output years from now on a whim.

Dollars to donuts most of these are just fishing for a quick shakedown buck and wouldn't be able to prove your work is their output in court.

replies.author: jonnygravity
replies.body:
I think that's probably largely true, but:

1. I think watermarking is pretty easy to do now since Ant started publishing so much information about how they do it  
2. I'm not sure if it's legally sufficient, but they can certainly prove a paper trail by showing their logs of your usage

That said, I agree it's mostly shakedown motivated and probably pretty easy to fly under the radar in most cases.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
I doubt the logs point to anything meaningful about a specific asset though, especially without a watermark.

"You generated an asset from our platform" only matters if they can prove this *specific* asset was used against the license.  For all they know you tossed that asset in the bin without direct proof that the individual output is the logged output

replies.author: Rashere
replies.body: I wouldn't bet on it. They're seeing the same gains from AI as other devs. Adding watermarking may be easy now.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
It may be, but a lot of these platforms are fly by night, vibe coded wrappers for custom comfyui workflows.  They're quick cash grabs, not legit companies capable of developing their own robust watermarking on the level of SynthID.

That and almost certainly many of them are wrapping open weight models as part of their service that *they* are in violation of the licensing for.

These platforms are a dime a dozen and it's the Wild West.  There's more snake oil salesman than anywhere else. I wouldn't trust any of them unless they can explicitly demonstrate the watermarking.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
The court won't care in the first place, at least if you're American. [The output of generative AI cannot be copyrighted](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/f237e6c7/is-the-output-of-the-generative-ai-system-protected-by-intellectual-property-rights).

> As at the date of this publication, courts which have considered the intellectual property rights concerning ‘works’ or the Output of generative AI have considered the issue in the context of an Output that is exclusively created by generative AI. In that context, the courts have concluded that the Output is not entitled to any copyright or patent protection under US law, as authorship or inventorship is limited to human beings. 
>
> Copyright: Copyright can protect only material that is the product of human creativity. Most fundamentally, the term ‘author,’ which is used in both the US Constitution and the US Copyright Act, excludes non-humans. The US Copyright Office’s registration policies and regulations reflect statutory and judicial guidance on this issue.
>
> Generally, individuals who use AI technology in creating a work may claim copyright protection for their own contributions to that work. Works that are solely created by AI technology are not able to be protected by copyright.

When you use these services, the only human input comes from you. Therefore, as soon as you have the bits, you can do whatever you want with those, and the service providing the generation has no rights to them. Neither do you though if you only prompted, but if you work on them extensively, you might get copyright for your own contributions.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
I think a really special and specific warning needs to be said about Suno and ElevenLabs, since those services are going to be tapped by so many people here: 

Their audio files have watermarking and a sonic signature that is embedded directly into the waveform of the audio you create. If you rip music or sounds from those platforms using recording software, the audio you ripped still has the watermark and sonic signature in it. 

It is completely trivial for the service provider to check that. 

While commercial success is extremely unlikely, it is - in my opinion - the height of stupidity to decide not to pay the $20 or whatever for the service. Because if you DO get commercial success, that can all literally be ruined overnight if you used ripped Suno or ElevenLabs and they check for their watermark.

Nobody here likes these bullshit IP laws and proprietary protection technology, but not liking it doesn't make it not exist, and you don't want to be having the conversation with a lawyer and/or a judge in a small claims court about how you just don't like the law, so you didn't think it applied to you.

replies.author: jonnygravity
replies.body: Agreed 100% and exactly why I put together Respawnstack and shared this post. I think it's really easy to overlook the risk. Putting in a ton of work to build a game only to get crushed by some stupid IP issue is the last thing you want to happen.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
Unless you live in China, it doesn't matter: [Generated content cannot be copyrighted](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10922). Legally, Suno or ElevenLabs have nothing to stand on.

> In March 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit affirmed the district court's decision in Thaler v. Perlmutter, holding that the Copyright Act "requires all eligible work to be authored in the first instance by a human being."
>
> May Humans Copyright Works That They Create Using AI?
>
> Assuming that copyrightable works require a human author, works created by humans with the assistance of generative AI might be entitled to copyright protection depending on the nature of human involvement in the creative process. As discussed below, the Copyright Office has sought to delineate what authors must do to satisfy the human-authorship requirement when using generative AI.

I guess you may have broken their terms of service or something so they can ban you, but by that time you already have what you need, and can make another account if you need more.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
I have given you the actual legal rulings. Not some vague terms of service, but what US courts have decided, when challenged to solve these cases. And the end result is clear: Generated content cannot be copyrighted.

But you do realize that none of this stuff is legally safe? At least Suno is trained on copyrighted content and is facing various lawsuits. The copyright status of both training generative models and using their output may vary globally.

If you want to play it safe, use licensed non-AI soundtrack services, or wait a few years until the dust settles around these new ones.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
First of all, Suno is a music generation service. The lawsuit about books, at least one of them, was against Anthropic.

There are currently [eight active lawsuits against Suno AI](https://ailawsuittracker.com/companies/suno/), another two have been settled.

Here is one [open lawsuit against Suno](https://www.cbc.ca/music/socan-suno-ai-lawsuit-9.7328609), from just a month ago:

> The Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada (SOCAN) has filed a lawsuit against Suno, alleging that the AI music generator has infringed the performing rights of music in SOCAN’s repertoire.
>
> SOCAN is the largest member-based music rights organization in Canada, with more than 200,000 songwriters, composers and music publishers. In the lawsuit, SOCAN lists a sample of 150 publicly available Suno outputs that have replicated songs by SOCAN’s members.

Here is [another one](https://variety.com/2026/biz/news/round-hill-music-sues-suno-anthropic-copyright-infringement-1236837467/) from August:

> The independent music publisher Round Hill Music sued Suno and Anthropic, accusing the two AI companies in a federal court in California of infringing its copyright by illegally scraping hundreds of its songs to train their models without permission.
>
> Round Hill, which owns the rights to songs such as Bonnie Tyler’s “Total Eclipse of the Heart, the Goo Goo Dolls’ “Iris” and more than 10,000 other compositions and recordings, claimed the two companies’ decision to lift the recordings violated the Copyright Act through its scraping.

You have shown enough of your expertise and should be quiet now.

comments.author: RemarkableWish2508
comments.body:
Fun fact: most of that is BS.

Generative AI doesn't apply new copyright, meaning the company can not "own" the output. In fact, if you upload anything for the AI to use in the generation, it's the copyright of whatever you uploaded (hopefully, assigned to you) that will be inherited by the output. They need a license *from you* to do anything with it!

That license grant is most likely in the ToS, otherwise you could sue them if they used your content, even remixed by a generative AI, without your permission... but yeah, the output is still not theirs.

What a platform can do when you break their ToS, is ban you and sue for breach of contract, not for the IP of the generations. That is still relevant, and you should check the ToS for that case, but generally they can only sue for actual financial losses, which in this case would be the cost of the lost subscription (beware of clauses about who pays legal costs, though).
